etymologies.etymologyHTML: Verb is from Middle English troublen, trublen, turblen, troblen, borrowed from Old French troubler, trobler, trubler, metathetic variants of tourbler, torbler, turbler, from Vulgar Latin *turbulō, from Latin turbula (“disorderly group, a little crowd or people”), diminutive of turba (“stir; crowd”). The noun is from Middle English truble, troble, from Old French troble, from the verb.

definitions.definition: A distressing or dangerous situation.
A difficulty, problem, condition, or action contributing to such a situation.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book XI”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Lest the fiend  […]  some new trouble raise.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Foul whisperings are abroad; unnatural deeds / Do breed unnatural troubles.

definitions.definition: A person liable to place others or themselves in such a situation.

quote.citation: 2021, Taylor Swift, Max Martin, Shellback (lyrics and music), “I Knew You Were Trouble (Taylor's Version)”, in Red (Taylor's Version)‎[1], performed by Taylor Swift:
quote.text: ’Cause I knew you were trouble when you walked inSo shame on me no-ow

definitions.definition: The state of being troubled, disturbed, or distressed mentally; unease, disquiet.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XL, page 63:
quote.text: Yet oft when sundown skirts the moor⁠An inner trouble I behold,⁠A spectral doubt which makes me cold,That I shall be thy mate no more,  […]

definitions.definition: Objectionable feature of something or someone; problem, drawback, weakness, failing, or shortcoming.
Violent or turbulent occurrence or event; unrest, disturbance.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “I don’t know how you and the ‘head,’ as you call him, will get on, but I do know that if you call my duds a ‘livery’ again there’ll be trouble. It’s bad enough to go around togged out like a life saver on a drill day, but I can stand that ’cause I'm paid for it. What I won’t stand is to have them togs called a livery.  […] ”

definitions.definition: Efforts taken or expended, typically beyond the normal required.

quote.citation: 1850, William Cullen Bryant, Letters of a Traveller:
quote.text: She never took the trouble to close them.
Indeed, by the report of our elders, this nervous preparation for old age is only trouble thrown away.

definitions.definition: Difficulty in doing something.
Health problems, ailment, generally of some particular part of the body.
A malfunction.
Liability to punishment; conflict with authority.
(mining) A fault or interruption in a stratum.
(Cockney rhyming slang) Wife. Clipping of trouble and strife.
(slang, dated) An unplanned, unwanted or undesired pregnancy.

quote.citation: 1971, Bob Stone (lyrics and music), “Gypsies, Tramps and Thieves”, performed by Cher:
quote.text: I never had schoolin’ but he taught me well / With his smooth southern style / Three months later I’m a gal in trouble / And I haven’t seen him for a while.

definitions.definition: (transitive, now rare) To disturb, stir up, agitate (a medium, especially water).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 5:4:
quote.text: For an Angel went downe at a certaine season into the poole, and troubled the water:

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book X”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, line 1100:
quote.text: God looking forth will trouble all his Hoſt

definitions.definition: (transitive) To mentally distress; to cause (someone) to be anxious or perplexed.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 12:27:
quote.text: Now is my soule troubled, and what shall I say? Father, saue me from this houre, but for this cause came I vnto this houre.

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i], page 281, column 2:
quote.text: Take the Boy to you: he ſo troubles me, / ’Tis paſt enduring.

quote.citation: 1693, [John Locke], “§65”, in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], →OCLC, page 68:
quote.text: Never trouble your ſelf about thoſe Faults in them, which you know Age will cure.

definitions.definition: (transitive) In weaker sense: to bother or inconvenience.
(transitive, of ailments, etc.) To physically afflict.
(reflexive or intransitive) To take pains to do something; to bother.
(intransitive) To worry; to be anxious.

quote.citation: 1946, Bertrand Russell, History of Western Philosophy, I.26:
quote.text: Why trouble about the future? It is wholly uncertain.
